---
title: "Stage 0 — map the protocol to ICH M11"
---

Reading an existing protocol against a fixed list of the things a protocol is supposed to
contain. Nothing is changed yet: this stage only establishes what the document does and does not
say, and where it says it.

## What this is

ICH M11 is a template for the clinical trial protocol: fourteen sections, and in the merged
electronic version 303 data elements, 216 of them Required, each carrying a CDISC code.
Mapping means deciding, element by element, which piece of the existing protocol answers it —
and recording the ones nothing answers.

## What you do

Read the source protocol against the element list and write the mapping down. The output is a
table, not an edit: element, where it is satisfied, or *absent*.

The absences are the interesting half, so record them with the same care as the matches.

## What you should see

A mapping document, and a count of required elements the protocol does not supply.

Expect that count to be substantial on any protocol not written to M11 in the first place. It
is a measure of the distance between two conventions, not of how good the protocol is.

## What to look out for

**Most of what looks missing is misplaced.** The commonest case: M11 §3.1.1 wants the estimand
*in the protocol*, and five of its seven required elements are ICH E9(R1) estimand attributes —
but the long-standing convention is to define estimands in the statistical analysis plan
instead. A protocol written that way fails a stack of required elements while the study itself
is perfectly well specified. Record such an element as *absent here, held in that document*
rather than as missing, or the mapping reads as an indictment when it is a translation.

**Resist fixing anything at this stage.** The urge to correct the protocol while mapping it is
strong, and it destroys the measurement: once you have edited, you can no longer say what the
protocol did say, and the count becomes a count of your own edits.

**Expect the same element in several places, disagreeing.** A synopsis, a body section and an
appendix will each carry a version of the population, or the randomisation ratio, and they will
not always agree. Which one is authoritative is a decision, and it should be a recorded one.

**Map the whole of a section, not the part that feeds your endpoint.** Reading selectively
means the first thing you learn about the rest is that it does not fit, usually much later.
